questions.q: What is the core principle that gives an ablation study its value?
options: Changing as many components as possible at once to save compute
Changing exactly one component while holding everything else fixed, to isolate its effect
Running the ablated variant for fewer training steps to save time
Comparing against a randomly chosen baseline each time
questions.explain: An ablation isolates a single cause by changing only one thing from the full model's config. If more than one thing changes, the result measures a combined effect rather than attributing the change to one component.

questions.q: Why does the lesson warn against giving an ablated variant a different training budget (e.g. fewer steps because it 'converges faster')?
options: Different training budgets are always required for a valid ablation
It confounds wall-clock convenience with a genuine performance difference, unless the claim is specifically about training speed
Training budgets have no effect on the final metric
It makes the experiment run faster, which is the only goal
questions.explain: Matching steps or compute (not wall-clock convenience) across variants is necessary unless the claim being tested is specifically about training speed — otherwise the comparison conflates two different things.

questions.q: Why should an ablation table report results across multiple seeds with mean and variance rather than a single point estimate?
options: Multiple seeds are only needed for the baseline, not the ablated variant
A small difference on a single seed could be noise rather than a real effect, so variance is needed to judge if the gap is meaningful
Reporting variance is a formatting convention with no bearing on the claim's validity
Single point estimates are always more accurate than averaged results
questions.explain: Without variance, a reader can't tell whether an observed gap (e.g. 0.3 points) reflects a real effect or just noise between seeds. Reporting mean ± std across multiple seeds lets the reader judge whether the effect exceeds the noise.

questions.q: According to the lesson, how should the baseline for an ablation be chosen?
options: Always use the paper's full model as the baseline, regardless of the claim being tested
The baseline should match the specific claim being tested -- e.g. full model minus the component in question, for an internal-component claim
The baseline should always be a prior published method, never a version of your own model
Baseline choice doesn't affect what an ablation can prove
questions.explain: For an internal-component claim ('does X matter'), the correct baseline is the full model with X removed vs. present under identical conditions. Using a weak prior-method baseline to make that kind of claim (or vice versa) is called out as a common way results get over-read.

questions.q: What does the lesson suggest doing when a component is so load-bearing that removing it produces a degenerate, untrainable model?
options: Report the degenerate result anyway as the official ablation
Skip the ablation entirely with no substitute
Use a controlled, weaker substitute variant instead of a true removal, since that's a more honest comparison
Increase the learning rate until the degenerate model trains successfully
questions.explain: When true removal of a component can't produce a meaningful trainable model, substituting a weaker but still functional variant gives a more honest comparison than an ablation that can't actually run.
